extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literature, playwrights, and critics
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative standards for composing tragedy (especially the tragic hero and dramatic structure), drawn from an academic treatment of Aristotle's Poetics and its reception. Covers unity, characterization, hamartia, catharsis, and related dramaturgical principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Action (controlling law of the drama)
rubrics_metrics.description: The failures and successes of the modern stage alike prove the truth of the Aristotelian principle, that Unity of Action is the higher and controlling law of the drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unity of Action should govern dramatic construction: the plot must hang together as a single coherent action. Other rules (time/place) must be subordinate to the unity of action; do not let formal constraints (e.g., imposed unities of time/place) fracture the causal or emotional development of the plot. Examples/anti-patterns: French dramatists who subordinated unity of action to the Unities of Time and Place compressed events artificially, cutting short natural development and violating inward logic of character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unities of Time and Place are secondary
rubrics_metrics.description: The Unities of Time and Place, so far as they can claim any artistic importance, are of secondary and purely derivative value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use time and place flexibly as tools that may enhance the unity of action, but avoid letting them dictate or distort the narrative. The poet's art may freely handle place and time; the imagination expects internal consistency rather than literal calendrical accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not cheat the imagination with puerile devices
rubrics_metrics.description: The imagination is not to be cheated by puerile devices into the belief that its world is the world of reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain internal plausibility and integrity of the imagined world. Poetic licence must not rely on trivial contrivances that break the audience's willing suspension of disbelief. Instead, create effects such that 'we forget all time' through artful handling rather than mechanical tricks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve the inward logic / inner consistency of character and events
rubrics_metrics.description: The external rule was thus observed, but at the cost of that inward logic of character and events which is prescribed by the Poetics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure characters behave according to motivations and causal chains established in the play. Avoid forcing characters into places or actions merely to satisfy formal constraints (e.g., to avoid scene-changes), because this undermines dramatic credibility and emotional payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy must produce katharsis: pity and fear
rubrics_metrics.description: The function of tragedy is to produce the katharsis of pity and fear; pity being felt for a person who, if not wholly innocent, meets with suffering beyond his deserts; fear being awakened when the sufferer is a man of like nature with ourselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct plot and character types and catastrophes specifically to elicit pity and fear. If either emotion is absent (or replaced by mere moral satisfaction), the distinctively tragic effect is lost. The plot should give 'full satisfaction' to these emotions—i.e., produce the proper cathartic response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid an eminently good (perfectly blameless) protagonist
rubrics_metrics.description: The spectacle of a man eminently good undergoing the change from prosperous to adverse fortune awakens neither pity nor fear. It shocks or repels us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A perfectly blameless sufferer tends to repel rather than move an audience because the sense of outraged justice can displace pity. Such characters often lack the dramatic tensions or motives that generate tragedy. (Discussion: Antigone is a special case debated by critics.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making the wicked prosper (bad man rising to prosperity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The bad man who experiences the contrary change from distress to prosperity: Pity and fear are here alike wanting. Even the sense of justice is unsatisfied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Triumph of wickedness offends the sense of justice and fails to produce tragic pity or fear; avoid using such arcs as central tragic plots. They may be realistic, but they introduce aesthetic disturbance rather than the harmonised causal form expected in tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid centring tragedy on the overthrow of an utter villain as the moral-satisfaction end
rubrics_metrics.description: The overthrow of the utter villain— a catastrophe that satisfies the moral sense—is lacking in the higher and distinctively tragic qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punishment of pure villainy may gratify moral feeling but does not ordinarily produce the mixed pity-and-fear required for tragedy. If using villain-centred drama, elevate the portrayal (see criterion on dignified villainy) or integrate with wider tragic motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal tragic hero: mixed moral composition, 'like ourselves', yet elevated
rubrics_metrics.description: He is not eminently good or utterly bad; he 'morally stands midway between the two extremes' and is 'a man of noble nature, like ourselves in elemental feelings and emotions; idealised, indeed, but with so large a share of our common humanity as to enlist our eager interest and sympathy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a protagonist who combines nobility or eminence (rank/fortune elevated enough to make catastrophe striking) with human fallibility. The hero should be recognisably similar to the audience (ὅμοιος) so pity and fear are possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hero should be illustrious in rank/fortune
rubrics_metrics.description: He is, moreover, illustrious in rank and fortune; the chief motive... being that the signal nature of the catastrophe may be more strikingly exhibited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grant the protagonist a sufficiently high station or significance so that the fall registers as dramatic and remarkable. The scale of the catastrophe amplifies the tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic misfortune should arise from hamartia (a great flaw or error), not deliberate vice
rubrics_metrics.description: He is involved in misfortune, not, however, as the result of deliberate vice, but through some great flaw of character or fatal error in conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the calamity to stem from an error—intellectual, accidental, or a moral frailty—rather than from sheer malice. The error (ἁμαρτία/hamartia) should be significant enough to plausibly lead to catastrophe, and allow for sympathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hamartia has multiple senses: error of judgement, passion-driven act, or character defect
rubrics_metrics.description: The word ἁμαρτία... admits of various shades of meaning: an error due to inadequate knowledge; an act committed in anger or passion; a defect of character distinct from vice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be precise about the kind of hamartia you employ and its moral implications. Any of these forms can justify tragic suffering; the key is that the error is not deliberate wickedness and that it plausibly precipitates the catastrophe. Examples: Oedipus (chain of errors/unconscious offence), Othello (passion), Macbeth (ambition as taint).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic ending (unhappy ending) is central to tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: The stress laid in this chapter on the unhappy ending is the key... The saying... is directly connected by Aristotle with the preference of the poet for the true tragic ending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An unhappy or disastrous conclusion is necessary for producing the full tragic effect; 'happy endings' or reconciliations tend toward comedy and dilute tragic catharsis. While audiences may prefer happy resolutions, a true tragedy risks that preference to achieve aesthetic ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic character needs initiative and passionate energy
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic character implies some self-assertive energy... Goodness... is apt to be immobile and uncombative. In refusing to strike back it brings the action to a standstill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid protagonists who are purely self-effacing or passively good; dramatic interest requires initiative that propels action and provokes responses from other characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Powerful or 'grand' villainy may be tragic if artistically portrayed
rubrics_metrics.description: Wickedness on a grand scale, resolute and intellectual, may raise the criminal above the commonplace and invest him with a sort of dignity... The wreck of such power excites...tragic sympathy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If centring on depravity, depict it with psychological and artistic complexity (e.g., Shakespeare's Richard III) so that awe or tragic grandeur can replace ordinary moral repulsion. This is risky and requires exceptional genius to retain tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contrast and complementary characters (light and shade)
rubrics_metrics.description: The wider law which demands the light and shade of contrasted characters—characters either standing out against one another in strong relief, or each forming the complement of the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose ensembles with complementary ethical types to heighten dramatic interest and moral/aesthetic complexity (pairs like Antigone/Ismene, Hamlet/Laertes, Brutus/Antony). A 'gratuitously bad' character may be justified when needed by dramatic motive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy should work by reading as well as performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle requires a good tragedy to produce its proper effect merely by reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the play's structure, language, and causal development convey the tragic effect without full reliance on stage spectacle. While stage representation can amplify certain effects (Euripides noted), the written drama must still carry the emotional logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic conflict may arise from external fate or internal moral forces
rubrics_metrics.description: The collision will be one between external forces outside the control of the human will... or will be one between internal moral forces, the scene of the conflict being the heart of man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either an inevitable external fate or an internal moral collision (struggles of conscience, divided will) can furnish the necessary tragic conflict. Choose the form that best serves the project's themes; both can produce catharsis if causally coherent and emotionally compelling.
